source: Authored by hand, NOT by author_flight.py. That tool authors an incoming flight from a passer position, and this drill has no incoming flight: the athlete starts with the ball.
startsWithTheBallNote: THE AUTHORING RULE FOR ANY DRILL THAT STARTS WITH THE BALL, followed here for the third time. Put BOTH keys where the ball actually is, in her hands, and name the smallest tidy arrival. DO NOT INVENT AN INCOMING FLIGHT TO SATISFY THE arrival FIELD. Both failure modes are guarded mechanically in test_starts_with_the_ball.py.
arrivalNote: A formality, not a catch. arrival names the frame possession transfers, and for a pass that already happened before the drill began. 0.0 is refused by load_ball, which requires release < arrival, so 0.02 is the smallest tidy value.

keys.name: in_her_hands
keys.note: Where the ball is when the drill starts, at her chest.

keys.name: still_in_her_hands
keys.note: The same place. A flight of zero length is the honest description of a ball that never flew.

launchTargetNote: PROVISIONAL, like every other authored number in this pack. THE LAUNCH IS AIMED AT THE FLOOR POINT, not at the receiver, so that this file needs no change on the day the engine gains a floor. THE ARITHMETIC, with its inputs. The stance frame is anchored at the chest as she stands at phase 0, measured at 126.32 cm, and the court is y = 0, so the floor sits at up = -126.32 / 52.68 = -2.3979 arm lengths. The manual's step 4 asks for the bounce 'approximately 1m in front of receiver'; on the manual's own lower bound of 'Area: Court (5-7m)' that puts the bounce 4.00 m ahead, which is 400 / 52.68 = 7.593 arm lengths. AT THE UPPER BOUND OF 7 m the bounce point would be 6.00 m ahead, 11.3895 arm lengths, and a coach may prefer it; 5 m is authored because the manual states the range and this is its near end. across is 0.0 because the bounce is in front of her, not to a side; the ball travels sideways during the CARRY and is released back on the midline.
launchSpeedNote: PROVISIONAL AND IT INHERITS AN OPEN QUESTION. 600 cm/s is author_flight.DEFAULT_SPEED_CM, the one speed the whole library uses, recorded in docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md as having no coach, no measurement and no source. Authoring a different number here would invent a second unsourced constant. IT IS THE HORIZONTAL COMPONENT; the vertical is solved so the ball reaches the target. A target BELOW the release does not by itself make the vertical downward, which a first draft of this note assumed and the measurement below disproves: it is downward only if the throw is fast enough that the ball would otherwise overshoot the drop. AND ON THIS DRILL THE CONSTANT PRODUCES A VISIBLY WRONG THROW, which is a sharper form of that open question than the two passes before it. Measured, and CORRECTED after a review: a first version of this note computed every figure over 400.0 cm, which is the target's distance FROM HER CHEST and not the flight's own span. THE BALL LEAVES 49.5 cm AHEAD OF HER CHEST, so the span is 350.5 cm. On the true span, 600 cm/s needs a vertical of +95.37 cm/s — the ball is still lobbed UPWARD at the floor, arcing from 111.7 up to 116.3 before it falls. A free fall from 111.7 cm takes 0.477 s, so the throw is only downward above 735 cm/s; the library's 600 is 0.82 of that. A BOUNCE PASS IS DRIVEN AT THE FLOOR, NOT LOBBED AT IT. The constant is left at 600 rather than corrected here, because authoring a second unsourced number is the fault this drill is trying not to repeat, and because the right value is a coach's or a measurement's. Recorded in the ledger beside the 5 m and 7 m apex figures.
noFloorNote: AND THE BALL DOES NOT STOP THERE. The engine has no floor: possession.py integrates a released ball as one unbroken parabola and nothing clamps it. Measured with the engine's own formula over the flight's true span of 350.5 cm — the floor point is 4.00 m from her CHEST and the ball leaves 49.5 cm ahead of it — the ball crosses the court at 0.584 s, exactly 400.0 cm from her chest, and is 8.5 m BELOW it by 1.5 s. THE CLIP HIDES THIS RATHER THAN FIXING IT: the release is at frame 76 of 96, which the definition writes as phase 0.80 and the exported clip as hit 0.7920, and the flight the clip then holds is 19 intervals at 60 frames per second, frame 76 to frame 95 = 0.3167 s. So the last frame comes 1.84 times too early and the ball is 0.268 s short of the floor. THE INTERVAL COUNT IS PART OF THE FIGURE: an earlier version of this note gave the flight as 0.32 s, which does not produce 0.268 when subtracted from 0.5842. The other two passes DO complete inside their clips, at frames 93 and 94 of 95. A viewer sees a ball still descending. Refer to docs/BOUNCE_PASS_INSTRUMENT_AUDIT.md.
